gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much wall energy a full charge takes or what that does to the fastest possible time. StorageReview measured 1,180 Wh from the wall to fill the 1,024 Wh EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus, about 87 % efficient. Because charging stops at 100 % but the losses still come out of the wall, the fastest possible full charge, with no slow-down near full, is 1,180 Wh ÷ max AC input. That works out to about 44 min for the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 at 1,600 W and 47 min for the DELTA 3 Plus at 1,500 W. It would be about 59 min for a 1,024 Wh unit capped at 1,200 W, such as the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2, which leaves no room to finish in under an hour.
standout_why: Compared against Dealectric's own page, testedwatts.com/how-long-to-charge, amphourly.com/best-mid-size-power-station and outdoorgearlab.com/best-power-station; thiswatt.com and unpluggedwatts.com failed to load (certificate error). TestedWatts gives maker times and input watts only, with no amps, efficiency or circuit maths beyond 15 A × 120 V ≈ 1,800 W. Amphourly gives maker times and weights; the fetch tool's summary also showed Wh ÷ minutes and amps at 120 V, but I couldn't tell whether those figures came from the page or from the summarizer. OutdoorGearLab gives measured Wh/hr and usable Wh but no wall-energy or loss figure. Dealectric's page already has about 13 A at 120 V and the 1,800 W circuit note, but no wall Wh per charge and no fastest-possible time for each model's input cap. None of these pages works out the best-case time from wall energy and the input cap, which is what tells you whether a unit can finish in under an hour at all.
decides: It backs the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 as the pick. It has the most headroom: about 44 min is its fastest possible time, against a 49 min claim and a 60 min target, so about 11 min of its claimed charge goes to slowing near full. The DELTA 3 Plus can't beat about 47 min and claims 56. A 1,024 Wh unit capped at 1,200 W (BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 TurboBoost) can't beat about 59 min even if it never slowed near full. That rules it out as an under-an-hour answer and explains why BLUETTI only claims 80 % in 45 min. The same check should be run on the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (1,070 Wh), whose input cap I couldn't source: unless its charger is better than 89 % efficient, 1,200 W could not fill it in under an hour.

findings.label: Wall energy for one full recharge (measured)
findings.note: StorageReview: 'The unit required 1.18kWh (1,180Wh) to recharge fully'; the app showed it charging at its rated 1,500 W, displayed as 1.45 kW.

findings.label: Charging efficiency, wall to battery (derived)
findings.note: 1,024 Wh ÷ 1,180 Wh = 0.868; about 156 Wh, roughly 13 %, is lost as heat.

findings.label: Fastest possible full charge at max input (derived)
findings.note: 1,180 Wh ÷ 1,500 W × 60 = 47.2 min. The review lists AC input as '1500W max, full charge in 56 minutes'; the remaining 9 min goes to slowing near full.

findings.label: Circuit note (named reviewer)
findings.value: 1,500 W is 'ideal when using a 20A receptacle and circuit'
findings.note: The review says the app's charge-speed limit helps with '15A 120V plugs' and 'overloaded circuits'. 1,500 W ÷ 120 V = 12.5 A.

findings.label: Fastest possible full charge at UltraFast input (derived)
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen2 - Anker SOLIX US
findings.note: Anker lists 1,024 Wh, 'AC Power (UltraFast Charging)' 1,600 W, '0 - 100% in Just 49 Min', UltraFast activated in the app. 1,180 Wh (DELTA 3 Plus wall energy, used as a stand-in for the same 1,024 Wh LFP capacity) ÷ 1,600 W × 60 = 44.3 min. Even with zero losses: 1,024 ÷ 1,600 × 60 = 38.4 min.

findings.note: 1,600 W ÷ 120 V = 13.3 A; 1,200 W ÷ 120 V = 10 A. Within a 15 A outlet, but leaves about 1.7 A for anything else on the circuit.

findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen2 - Anker SOLIX US (plus the StorageReview and BLUETTI pages above)
findings.note: 1,024 Wh ÷ 1 h ÷ max input: 1,024/1,600 = 0.64; 1,024/1,500 = 0.68; 1,024/1,200 = 0.85. Before conversion losses. The lower the share, the more room the unit has to slow near full and still finish within the hour.

unsourced: Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 AC input in Emergency mode (1,200 W on our page) and capacity: jackery.com returned HTTP 429 three times and storecheck also got HTTP 429. Both manual PDFs (mrsolar.com, hampshiregenerators.co.uk) came back as unreadable compressed binary, and I wasn't allowed to run a local PDF-to-text tool. If 1,200 W is confirmed: 1,070 Wh ÷ 1,200 W × 60 = 53.5 min with zero losses, and the charger would need to be better than 89 % efficient (1,070 ÷ 1,200) to finish within 60 min.

The zero-loss times are given alongside as a hard lower bound.
